A1.justification: Both PDFs describe UnHype and retain matching methods, experiments, equations, and figures. All 14 pages of v1 and 23 pages of v2, including their appendices, support comparison. Internal reporting inconsistencies do not prevent identifying the changes.

before.justification: Tables 1–4 report original UnHype experiments on object, nudity, and celebrity erasure, supported by qualitative examples and appendix evaluation protocols.

after.justification: V2 retains original UnHype experiments and adds adversarial evaluations, runtime measurements, multi-concept benchmarks, ablations, and failure cases.

M1.justification: The NV-Embed-v2 celebrity-conditioning variant described and evaluated in v1 Section 5.4 is dropped; v2 retains the CLIP variant already evaluated in v1. This is a limited removal of a model variant. The hypernetwork trajectory formulation, removal and retention losses, LoRA placement, and Stable Diffusion/Flux inference procedures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 adds simultaneous removal of ten Imagenette classes and ImageNet-Confuse5 evaluation across five groups of visually similar erased and preserved classes. It also adds adversarial I2P prompts and benign prompts containing nudity-related language. These substantially broaden task requirements and test conditions beyond the retained object, nudity, and celebrity evaluations.

E2.justification: Stable Diffusion nudity Table 2 adds AdvUn, Receler, CPE, and STEREO. New comparisons include RACE for robustness and timing, SalUn/SPM/SP for multi-object erasure, ScaPre for fine-grained erasure, and static LoRA for inference timing. The external comparator sets in the retained Flux and celebrity tables remain unchanged.

E3.justification: New protocols include 95 adversarial prompts per attack, ResNet-50 and UQ benchmark evaluation, fine-grained preservation metrics, controlled runtime comparisons, and parameter sweeps. Celebrity evaluation drops the larger-encoder configuration. Appendix C.1 changes object-erasure sampling from 50 to 200 images per prompt, but Section 5.2 still states 50 and Table 1 is unchanged; this establishes a reported protocol revision, not a confirmed rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds UnlearnDiffAtk and Ring-A-Bell robustness tests, benign-context failure cases, runtime analyses, and ablations of LoRA rank, removal/retention loss weighting, and mapping targets versus empty prompts. Neighbor-probe examples test collateral suppression. These substantially extend v1's synonym examples, although its larger-encoder comparison is removed.

E5.justification: V2 Table 8 newly reports inference-time means and standard deviations over 100 generations. Figures 7–9 also disclose qualitative seed counts or identifiers. The main erasure benchmarks still lack repeated-training-run uncertainty estimates or significance tests; UQ's cross-method normalization is not such an uncertainty estimate.

E6.justification: Table 1 is unchanged. Reported UnHype NudeNet totals change from 18 to 8 on Stable Diffusion and 38 to 32 on Flux, alongside revised FID/CLIP values. The celebrity CLIP row changes from Acce/Accs/Ho of 11.72/87.48/87.88 to 0.46/86.35/92.48, while the NV-Embed-v2 row disappears. V2 also adds attack success rates of 0.00% and 1.05%, benchmark results, timings, and ablation outcomes; these additions are not same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: Appendix D introduces the mathematical definition of UQ through sigmoid-normalized erasure and quality scores and their harmonic mean; Appendix E specifies the new benchmark's Overall Acc measure. The underlying method equations and existing harmonic-mean metrics are retained. No theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The abstract and central contribution of dynamic, semantically conditioned LoRA unlearning remain stable. The introduction narrows the efficiency contribution to computational savings through a single training run in the multi-concept regime, dropping the earlier explicit memory-savings claim.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive limitations concerning keyword-driven suppression of benign cosmetics, animal, and medical prompts. It explains how mapping targets protect neighboring concepts, interprets adversarial resistance through pooled CLIP conditioning, and qualifies efficiency advantages as amortization across concepts. These materially expand the mechanism discussion and applicability boundaries beyond v1's largely positive interpretation.

D1.justification: Appendix B.1 adds training and inference hardware, wall-clock measurements, image resolution, and sampler details. Appendices E–F disclose ranks, loss weights, and mapping choices. Original prompt lists, the training configuration table, and the repository link remain. V2 removes the explicit MS-COCO-10k label from the celebrity results table, reducing sample-count documentation there.

R1.justification: The related-work section and central positioning against static LoRA approaches are largely retained. Targeted additions cite adversarial methods and attacks, newer multi-concept work, and benchmark/evaluator sources, including STEREO, Ring-A-Bell, Li et al. (2025), and Deng et al. (2026). The discussion also qualifies the computational comparison with prior LoRA methods.

P1.justification: Localized rewrites clarify scalability, shorten inference explanations, and replace the celebrity encoder rationale. V2 adds experimental and appendix subsections, an impact statement, acknowledgements, and updated publication/affiliation text. Most existing exposition and the overall section order are retained; the added scientific material does not constitute a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: V2 adds substantial displays for adversarial performance, training/inference timing, new benchmarks, and ablations, plus Figures 7–12 showing failures and qualitative comparisons. Existing result tables gain highlighting and revised row structures. Figure 3 is relocated, and the training-prompt appendix is compacted; its retained prompt content is not newly added.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens empirical scrutiny of the retained method: Section 5.5 and Appendices B.1 and D–F test adversarial recovery, computational cost, simultaneous erasure, fine-grained preservation, and component sensitivity that v1 did not establish. Concrete benign-context failures also make the limitations more informative. The new 50-versus-200 sampling contradiction and limited uncertainty reporting temper confidence, but the gains in validation and transparency are substantial independently of the higher reported scores.
